messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Patricia Vance was fifty-eight when a routine industrial safety audit at a regional chemical processing plant turned catastrophic. She had been verifying ventilation schematics on an upper gantry when a pressure valve she had just inspected ruptured without warning. A sudden plume of volatile solvents erupted, carrying a sharp, acrid scent that instantly scorched her throat and lungs. The emergency fire suppression system misfired, igniting trapped vapors and sending a rolling wave of smoke and burnt insulation through the corridor. She remembered the heat pressing against her face, the disorienting haze, and the terrifying realization that she had miscalculated the airflow dynamics she was meant to oversee. When the fumes finally cleared, the lingering whiff of charred plastic and solvent clung to her clothes, imprinting a precise olfactory map of the catastrophe into her nervous system. In the months that followed, her physiological alarm system began to misfire at ordinary cues. A neighbor’s barbecue grill sparking across the street would instantly spike her heart rate, her palms dampening as her breath grew shallow. The smell of whiskey at a colleague’s desk triggered the same visceral lurch in her stomach that had accompanied the initial leak. Because her body reacted so violently to these olfactory reminders, she found herself unable to separate the present moment from the past danger. Every time a smoke alarm tested or a restaurant kitchen vented cooking fumes, the physical reactivity would surge first, which then amplified her perception of the smell as an imminent threat, making the burnt scent and the smoke cues feel increasingly urgent and unmanageable. This relentless physical alarm slowly eroded her confidence. She had come to believe that she could no longer rely on herself to navigate ordinary spaces safely. The memory of her flawed assessment on the gantry had solidified into a quiet conviction that she could never trust her own decisions, that a catastrophic mistake was always waiting to repeat itself. Worse, she felt a hollow detachment settling over her daily life; what frightened her most was the certainty that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the exposure had burned out her capacity for calm. These interpretations did not merely linger; they actively reshaped her internal landscape, convincing her that her own judgment was fundamentally compromised and that she was permanently disconnected from her former self. To manage this mounting distress, Patricia constructed rigid routines to compensate for what she perceived as her own unreliability. She would sit at her desk at the regional policy office and meticulously ruminate about how the plant’s safety protocols could have been designed differently, replaying the incident to find a variable she could have controlled. Her checking behaviors expanded into her home life; she would run through every room of her house twice, verifying windows and vents, before allowing herself to sleep. She also stopped watching television or browsing news sites, carefully avoiding any footage of chemical spills or factory fires, fearing that visual reminders would unravel her fragile composure. Within her professional work, the cycle dictated her daily reality. While drafting environmental compliance reports, the faint ozone scent of overheating office equipment would trigger a surge of adrenaline that left her trembling, forcing her to step into the stairwell until her breathing steadied. Each physical reaction she experienced in response to that stimulus fed back into her negative self-assessment, convincing her that her nervous system was permanently fractured. The more she ruminated on what went wrong and the more she checked her environment, the more convinced she became that her own judgment was unreliable. As her self-doubt deepened, the burnt scent of a car backfiring or the sharp tang of industrial cleaner no longer just startled her; it confirmed her growing belief that she was fundamentally compromised, which in turn made her hyperaware of environmental cues and kept her scanning for threats long after the danger had passed. Patricia, now sixty-one, finally sought help after her husband gently pointed out how her constant seat-shifting and refusal to leave the house for dinner had grown exhausting. She was terrified that she would never recover her sense of safety, yet she held onto the quiet hope that someone could help her untangle the fear from the facts and let her live without the weight of the past.
